newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline prices fall as supply fears fade.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline prices fall as supply fears fade.

text.p: Gasoline prices fell sharply Thursday amid talk that more supplies would be arriving soon at New York Harbour both from overseas and the U.S. Gulf.
Concern about supply tightness had recently sent prices soaring as a strong U.S. economy led to a particularly active summer driving season, stoking high gasoline demand.
Dealers said the price advance had made it more attractive to import gasoline into the United States.
There was also talk a prominent trader was sending large supplies to New York Harbour from the U.S. Gulf to satisfy delivery obligations under the NYMEX August contract.
"The market psychology has become bearish so the market is using the imminent cargo story as an excuse to sell," said Tim Evans, analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group in New York.
Gasoline for September delivery at the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) closed 1.73 cents a gallon lower at 64.33.
Meanwhile, September crude ended 37 cents a barrel lower at $20.09 and September heating oil ended 1.68 cents lower at 55.30 cents a gallon, in part tracking gasoline's decline.
Dealers also noted the market was bracing for the resumption of Iraqi oil sales. On Wednesday, Iraq's Oil Minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed said he expects Iraq to resume oil exports by mid-August.
The pricing formula for Iraq's "oil-for-food" plan with the U.N. was passed to the U.N. sanctions committee, which has until 1100 EDT Friday to raise any objections.
Otherwise, the formula is accepted, and Iraq can sell oil.
At the Chicago Board of trade soybeans fell sharply amid some signs that crops in key growing areas in the U.S. Midwest may get much needed rains.

"We're in the critical time frame for soybeans," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities. "We either make or break them in August. There's been no irreversable damage done to soybeans. If we get the (rain) there's a big probability that we will have above trend-line yields in soybeans."
Weather Services Corp meteorologist Joel Burgio said weekend storms would likely bring 0.25 to 0.75 inch of rain to the U.S. Midwest with 40 to 50 percent coverage.

But there was a slight chance that a second system brewing in the South would bring heavier precipitation, he said. Traders said other meteorologists also suggested more rains in some dry areas on the central Corn Belt.
An Iowa-based grain firm, Farmers Commodities Corp, also issued a higher than expected estimate for this year's U.S. soybean crop.

FCC put soybean output at 2.73 billion bushels, which if achieved would be a record crop. The forecast was also above the U.S. Department of Agriculture's latest estimate, issued in July, of 2.69 billion bushels.
USDA will revise its crop production estimate on Tuesday at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT.
CBOT soybeans for November delivery closed 21-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $6.28-1/2.
Cotton prices on the New York Cotton Exchange closed lower as crop boosting rains swept across west Texas.
Rains fell across the west Texas cotton growing region which encompasses about three million acres, Texas A & M cotton specialist Carl Anderson said.
"They were very beneficial for the region especially on the dryland," he said.
"Lamesa, Texas, a major cotton growing area, had 1.34 inches of rain during the last 24 hours," Weather Services Corp meteorologist Mike Palmerino said.
The Delta was also expected to receive beneficial rain in the next 48 hours with moderate temperatures, he said.
Cotton for December delivery closed 1.00 cent a lb lower at 74.40 cents a lb.
